text:
Although some people believe that imposing harsher custodial terms on juvenile offenders is the most effective way to curb youth crime, I strongly disagree. While serious offenses must be punished appropriately, longer prison sentences are generally a blunt instrument that does little to address the roots of offending. In most cases, prevention, rehabilitation, and targeted social support are far more effective in reducing criminal behavior among young people.

One major problem with extended imprisonment is that it often intensifies, rather than diminishes, criminal tendencies. Adolescents are still developing emotionally and cognitively, which means they are especially vulnerable to negative influences. When they spend long periods in correctional institutions, they may be exposed to older and more experienced offenders, learn antisocial attitudes, and emerge with even fewer legitimate opportunities than before. For example, a teenager incarcerated for repeated theft may leave prison with a stronger criminal network, interrupted schooling, and a permanent stigma that makes employment difficult, all of which increase the likelihood of reoffending.

By contrast, policies that tackle the underlying causes of youth crime can produce more lasting results. Many young offenders come from unstable homes, struggle at school, or live in neighborhoods where violence is common. Interventions such as counseling, mentoring, vocational training, and closely supervised community service can help them build self-discipline and a sense of responsibility without severing their ties to education and family life. In several countries, diversion programs for first-time offenders have reduced repeat offending by combining accountability with practical support, showing that reform is often more productive than prolonged detention.

This is not to say that prison should never be used. Dangerous or persistent offenders may need to be removed from society for public safety, and a short custodial sentence can sometimes mark the seriousness of a crime. Nevertheless, presenting longer sentences as the best solution is misguided. Youth crime is more effectively reduced by measures that change behavior, expand opportunity, and prevent vulnerable adolescents from entering the criminal justice system in the first place.

The question of who should bear the cost of maintaining cultural institutions has long divided opinion. Some argue that public money should sustain museums and galleries, while others maintain that they ought to be financially self-sufficient through admission fees. Although both positions have merit, I believe that governments should provide the core funding, supplemented by modest revenue from visitors.

Those who favor ticket sales make a reasonable case. Taxpayers include many people who never visit a museum, and it can seem unfair to ask them to subsidize a pastime they do not enjoy. Moreover, institutions that depend on their own income have a strong incentive to keep exhibitions fresh and attract larger audiences. Several private museums in the United States, for example, have built successful businesses by offering immersive displays, cafes, and well-stocked gift shops, which in turn finance new acquisitions.

Nevertheless, relying entirely on admission fees carries serious risks. Museums are custodians of national heritage, and their work, such as conservation, research, and education, rarely generates an immediate profit. If survival depended on revenue alone, curators might favor crowd-pleasing blockbusters over scholarly but less popular collections. High prices could also exclude low-income families, widening the cultural gap between rich and poor. The experience of Britain is instructive: when the government abolished entrance charges at its national museums in 2001, visitor numbers rose sharply, and many first-time visitors came from less affluent backgrounds.

In my view, the most sensible solution is a mixed model. Public funding should guarantee the essential functions of preservation and free access to permanent collections, since these benefit society as a whole by strengthening education and national identity. At the same time, institutions can charge for special exhibitions, host events, and seek private sponsorship, which would reduce the burden on taxpayers and encourage innovation.

In conclusion, although charging visitors has some advantages, cultural institutions serve a public purpose that markets alone cannot protect. Government support, combined with carefully chosen additional income, offers the fairest and most sustainable approach.

In many parts of the world, school leavers choose to postpone higher education or employment for a year. Although this break can involve certain risks, I believe its benefits are greater, provided that the time is used purposefully. A well-planned gap year can foster maturity, clarify future goals, and develop practical skills that formal education often neglects.

The principal advantage is personal growth. At the end of high school, many teenagers are academically qualified for university but still uncertain about their interests, values, and long-term ambitions. A year spent traveling, volunteering, or living away from home can make them more independent and resilient, because they must manage money, time, and unfamiliar situations on their own. For example, a student who works on a community project overseas may return with greater confidence and a clearer sense of social responsibility, qualities that can improve both academic performance and later professional conduct.

A further benefit is that a temporary pause can lead to better educational and career decisions. Many young people enter degree programs simply because it is the expected next step, only to discover later that they have chosen the wrong subject. By contrast, relevant work experience can help them assess whether a field genuinely suits them. Someone who spends several months assisting in a hospital, for instance, may confirm a commitment to medicine or decide instead to pursue public health administration. In either case, the eventual choice is likely to be more informed.

Admittedly, there are disadvantages. Some young adults lose academic momentum, while others waste the year in unstructured leisure or find it difficult to resume studying. In addition, extended travel can be expensive and may widen inequality between those who can afford such opportunities and those who cannot. Nevertheless, these drawbacks are not inherent to the idea itself; they arise mainly when the period lacks structure or support.

Overall, the advantages of taking a year off exceed the disadvantages. When guided by clear objectives, this interval can transform inexperienced school graduates into more focused, capable, and motivated adults, which ultimately benefits both the individual and society.

Traffic congestion has become one of the most pressing challenges facing modern cities, wasting time, damaging health and harming economies. In my view, the problem stems chiefly from rapid urban growth combined with an overreliance on private cars, and it can be alleviated most effectively by investing in public transportation and by making driving more costly.

The first major cause is the steady expansion of urban populations without a matching expansion of road capacity. As people migrate to cities in search of employment, housing is often built on the outskirts, which forces residents to commute long distances. Lagos, for instance, has grown so quickly that its road network cannot absorb the daily influx of vehicles, and journeys of two hours are commonplace.

A second cause is the widespread dependence on private vehicles, which is encouraged by inadequate alternatives. Where buses are unreliable and trains are scarce, even those on modest incomes feel compelled to buy a car or motorbike. Because a single car occupies far more road space per passenger than a bus does, each additional driver intensifies the gridlock. Rising incomes in developing economies have only accelerated this trend.

Turning to solutions, the most effective measure is to build efficient, affordable and safe public transportation. When commuters can rely on frequent metro services, many will willingly leave their cars at home. Seoul, for example, reduced congestion in its center after it integrated its bus and subway systems and introduced dedicated bus lanes. Governments can also discourage unnecessary driving through congestion charges, as London has done since 2003, which cut central traffic volumes and generated revenue that was reinvested in transit.

In conclusion, congestion arises mainly from fast-growing populations and a heavy dependence on private cars. Authorities should respond by improving public transportation and by pricing road use sensibly, since these measures tackle the underlying causes rather than merely adding more lanes that soon fill up again.

Around the world, smaller languages are vanishing at an alarming rate as their speakers shift to more dominant tongues. This trend is driven mainly by economic and social pressures, as well as by the growing reach of national education systems and digital media. In my view, the decline does matter greatly, because when a language disappears, societies lose far more than a means of communication.

One major reason for language loss is that speaking a powerful language often brings clear practical advantages. Parents naturally want their children to succeed in school and employment, so they encourage them to use the national or global language instead of the local one. Over time, the minority language is confined to older generations and eventually falls out of daily use. This pattern can be seen in many Indigenous communities, where younger people adopt English or Spanish because these languages dominate universities, government, and the labor market.

A second cause is cultural centralization in modern life. Television, social media, and online entertainment overwhelmingly operate in a handful of widely spoken languages, leaving little space for smaller ones. As a result, young people may associate their ancestral language with isolation or backwardness rather than opportunity. For example, if children consume all their music, films, and educational content in Mandarin or French, they are unlikely to develop fluency in a local language that has little presence in the digital world.

I strongly believe this loss is significant. Languages encode distinctive ways of seeing the world, including oral history, ecological knowledge, humor, and social values that are often impossible to translate fully. When a language dies, entire cultural memories can vanish with it. In addition, linguistic diversity, like biodiversity, makes humanity more resilient and intellectually rich. The disappearance of a small Arctic language, for instance, may also mean the loss of generations of precise knowledge about weather, ice, and survival in extreme conditions.

Admittedly, a shared language can improve national unity and international communication. Nevertheless, this benefit should not come at the cost of erasing linguistic heritage. Governments and communities should therefore support bilingual education and media production so that smaller languages can survive alongside more widely used ones.

issues.quote: Languages encode distinctive ways of seeing the world, including oral history, ecological knowledge, humor, and social values that are often impossible to translate fully.
issues.correction: Languages encode distinctive ways of seeing the world and carry oral history, ecological knowledge, humor, and social values that are often impossible to translate fully.
issues.reason: Oral history, ecological knowledge, etc. are not ways of seeing the world, so "including" is a loose, illogical link; the revised wording fixes this.
"also" is redundant and unidiomatic here, since the sentence adds no contrast to a prior mention.

adjudication.note: Stylistic preference; "including" and "also" are acceptable here.

text:
It is often claimed that artificial intelligence will soon outperform humans in most occupations, and that schools should therefore abandon career preparation. I agree only in part. Education should certainly place less emphasis on narrow vocational training, but it should not abandon the development of practical, career-relevant knowledge altogether.

The argument for moving away from specific career preparation is persuasive. Technology is reshaping the labor market so quickly that skills taught to a fifteen-year-old may be obsolete by the time that student graduates. Translators, bookkeepers, and paralegals, for instance, already compete with software that completes routine tasks in seconds. Schools that train students for a single profession risk equipping them with abilities that employers no longer value. A curriculum built around adaptability, critical thinking, and creativity is therefore a far safer investment.

Nevertheless, it would be unwise to discard career-oriented learning entirely. Students need concrete domains in which to practice general skills, because abstract thinking develops best through engagement with real problems. A student who studies basic engineering, for example, learns not only technical content but also how to analyze constraints and test solutions. Moreover, the claim that machines will do most jobs better is speculative. Roles requiring empathy, physical dexterity, or ethical judgment, such as nursing and teaching, remain difficult to automate, and societies will continue to need people trained for them.

A balanced approach is therefore the most sensible. Schools could introduce students to a broad range of fields, teach them how artificial intelligence works, and encourage them to use it as a tool rather than fear it as a rival. Finland, for instance, integrates project-based learning across subjects, allowing pupils to combine knowledge from several disciplines.

In conclusion, although rapid automation justifies a shift toward flexible, transferable skills, schools should not stop offering career-related education. The most effective model would blend broad intellectual foundations with practical exposure, preparing young people for a future that nobody can predict with confidence.

Whether parents ought to impose firm limits on children’s computer gaming or allow youngsters to regulate it themselves remains contentious. Although self-direction can help children develop independence, I believe parents should set clear boundaries, particularly when children are too young to judge the consequences of excessive play responsibly.

Those who favor allowing children to decide often argue that autonomy is an essential part of growing up. If every leisure activity is tightly supervised, children may struggle to learn moderation and self-discipline for themselves. In addition, many computer games are not merely frivolous entertainment; some promote problem-solving, teamwork, and persistence. For example, a child who manages time independently between homework, sports practice, and an hour of online gaming may gradually acquire the ability to prioritize tasks without constant adult intervention. From this perspective, freedom can be a practical lesson in responsibility.

Nevertheless, the case for parental control is stronger because children are especially vulnerable to habits they cannot easily regulate. Games are deliberately designed to be immersive, and without limits many young people will choose immediate pleasure over sleep, exercise, or study. This can undermine both physical health and academic performance. For instance, a ten-year-old who is permitted to play late into the night may arrive at school tired, inattentive, and increasingly dependent on gaming as a source of comfort. In such situations, expecting mature self-control from a child is unrealistic.

A balanced approach is therefore preferable, but the balance should be determined by parents, not children alone. Adults can establish reasonable rules, such as permitting gaming only after homework is completed and capping screen time on school nights, while still involving children in discussions about those rules. This preserves a degree of choice within a safe framework.

In conclusion, while giving children some say over their free time can encourage independence, parents should retain ultimate authority over how long computer games are played. Sensible limits protect children from excess while gradually teaching them how to manage freedom wisely.

The number of people living alone has risen sharply in recent decades, particularly in wealthy urban societies. Although this arrangement carries genuine risks, I believe that its benefits generally outweigh its drawbacks, provided that individuals remain connected to a wider community.

The most significant advantage of solitary living is the autonomy it affords. Residents can organize their schedules, finances and living spaces according to their own preferences, without negotiating with roommates or partners. This freedom is especially valuable for young professionals, who may need quiet surroundings to study or to build a career. Moreover, those who live alone often develop practical independence and emotional resilience. A graduate who must cook, budget and solve household problems unaided, for instance, tends to acquire a self-reliance that serves her well throughout adult life.

Another benefit is that living alone can improve the quality of relationships rather than diminish it. Because social contact is no longer automatic, people must make deliberate efforts to meet friends and relatives, and such encounters are frequently more meaningful as a result. In addition, the ability to retain a private refuge helps many individuals recover from the pressures of work, which supports their mental health.

Nevertheless, the disadvantages cannot be dismissed. Loneliness is the most serious of them, and it is a particular danger for elderly people whose spouses have died and whose children live far away. Research has linked chronic isolation to depression and cardiovascular disease, and a person who falls ill at home may go unnoticed for days. Living alone is also more expensive, since rent and utility bills are not shared, which places a heavy burden on low earners in cities such as London or Tokyo.

In conclusion, although isolation and higher costs are real concerns, the independence and personal growth that solitary living encourages are more important for most people. Governments and communities can reduce the harms by funding social programs for vulnerable residents, so that the advantages of living alone remain the dominant ones.

Plastic debris has become one of the gravest environmental threats of the modern era, particularly in marine ecosystems. In my view, this crisis stems chiefly from the enormous volume of disposable plastic produced for everyday convenience and from weak waste-management systems that allow discarded material to enter rivers and seas. Although the problem is severe, it can be substantially reduced through tighter regulation, better infrastructure, and changes in consumer behavior.

One major cause is the widespread dependence on single-use items, such as bottles, packaging, straws, and shopping bags. These products are cheap, lightweight, and durable, which makes them commercially attractive but environmentally disastrous. Because plastic does not biodegrade quickly, even a brief moment of use can result in decades of pollution. For example, takeaway food containers used for only minutes are often blown from open trash bins into waterways, where they fragment into microplastics and are later ingested by fish, seabirds, and turtles.

A second reason is that many cities and countries lack effective systems for collecting, sorting, and recycling waste. In places where landfills are poorly managed or disposal services are limited, rubbish is frequently dumped illegally or washed away during heavy rain. This is especially damaging near coasts and major rivers, which act as direct channels to the ocean. In parts of Southeast Asia, for instance, inadequate municipal collection has been identified as a key factor behind the vast quantities of plastic carried into the sea each year.

To address this issue, governments should first curb unnecessary plastic production by banning certain disposable products, taxing plastic packaging, and requiring manufacturers to use recyclable or compostable alternatives. At the same time, public authorities must invest in reliable waste collection, modern recycling facilities, and drainage filters that stop litter before it reaches open water. Public education is equally important: when consumers bring reusable bags and bottles, demand for throwaway items falls.

Ultimately, oceanic plastic pollution is driven by both overconsumption and poor disposal. If governments, industries, and individuals act together, the damage to marine life can be greatly diminished.

Children have become one of the most heavily courted audiences in modern marketing. Companies target them because young consumers influence family spending and form brand loyalties that can last a lifetime. Although this practice is troubling, I believe that a strict regulation of such advertising is preferable to a complete ban.

The commercial logic behind child-focused advertising is straightforward. Children rarely have large budgets of their own, but they exert considerable pressure on the adults who do. Parents often yield to persistent requests for toys, snacks, or electronic games, a phenomenon marketers call the "nag factor." Moreover, preferences acquired in childhood tend to endure. A child who grows up associating a particular cereal or sneaker brand with fun and belonging may remain a customer for decades, which makes early exposure a valuable long-term investment.

Nevertheless, the vulnerability of young audiences gives governments a strong reason to intervene. Children below a certain age cannot distinguish persuasion from entertainment, so they absorb commercial messages uncritically. This is especially harmful when the products promoted are unhealthy. Aggressive campaigns for sugary drinks and fast food have been linked to rising rates of childhood obesity, and the pressure to own fashionable possessions can foster anxiety and materialism among young people. Sweden and Quebec, for instance, restrict commercials directed at young children, and their experience shows that firm limits are workable.

However, an outright ban would be difficult to enforce and could have unintended consequences. Online content crosses national borders, and influencers can promote products in ways that evade traditional rules. Furthermore, many children's programs and educational websites depend on advertising revenue, so a total prohibition might reduce the quality or availability of free content. A more realistic approach would prohibit advertising for unhealthy foods during children's viewing hours, require clear labeling of sponsored posts, and fund media literacy lessons in schools.

In conclusion, companies target children because of their influence on household purchases and their potential as lifelong customers. Since children are especially impressionable, advertising should be tightly controlled, but targeted regulation and education offer a more effective solution than a blanket ban.

It is often argued that personal habits such as sorting household waste or reducing electricity use are insignificant in the face of climate change and pollution, and that meaningful progress depends entirely on states and major corporations. I partly disagree with this view. While large institutions undoubtedly possess the scale and resources required for systemic change, individual behavior remains an essential part of any effective environmental response.

On the one hand, governments and businesses are uniquely positioned to address the structural causes of ecological damage. Only public authorities can impose emissions standards, redesign transport systems, or invest in renewable energy infrastructure on a national scale. Likewise, multinational firms control vast supply chains and production processes, meaning that a single corporate decision can reduce waste or carbon output far more than thousands of households acting alone. For example, when a city government expands reliable public transit and a manufacturer shifts to low-carbon materials, the resulting reduction in emissions is both immediate and extensive.

However, it is mistaken to conclude that personal choices therefore matter little. Environmental problems are cumulative, arising from millions of daily decisions about consumption, travel, food, and energy use. If large numbers of people adopt more sustainable habits, the combined effect can be substantial. In many countries, widespread use of energy-efficient appliances and LED lighting has lowered household electricity demand significantly. Moreover, consumer preferences can pressure companies to change. The rapid growth of reusable products and plant-based foods, for instance, has been driven not by legislation alone but by consistent public demand.

Individual action also has an important political dimension. Citizens who care enough to modify their own lifestyles are often more likely to vote for green policies, join local campaigns, or support stricter regulation. In this way, personal responsibility can reinforce institutional reform rather than distract from it.

In conclusion, although governments and large companies carry the greatest responsibility because they can transform entire systems, individual actions are far from irrelevant. Environmental progress is most likely when policy, corporate practice, and everyday behavior work together.

The question of who should bear the cost of higher education is one of the most contested issues in public policy. While free tuition is often praised for promoting fairness, I believe that a system in which students contribute to their own studies, supported by generous grants and income-contingent loans, is more sustainable and ultimately more just.

Advocates of free university education argue that it opens doors for talented young people regardless of their family income. When tuition is eliminated, a gifted student from a poor household does not have to weigh potential academic success against the fear of crippling debt. Germany offers a telling example: after abolishing tuition fees in its public universities, it has attracted large numbers of domestic and international students and has benefited from a highly skilled workforce. Supporters also point out that graduates generate wider social gains, such as higher tax revenue and advances in medicine and technology, so society as a whole should share the expense.

Nevertheless, there are compelling reasons why students should pay at least part of the cost. Public budgets are finite, and funding universities entirely through taxation means that money is diverted from areas such as primary education and healthcare. Moreover, graduates typically earn considerably more over their lifetimes than non-graduates, so it seems unfair to ask a taxpayer who never attended university to subsidize those who will later enjoy higher salaries. In countries such as Australia, income-contingent loans address this concern effectively, since graduates repay their debt only once their earnings exceed a certain threshold. This arrangement protects those on low incomes while ensuring that universities receive stable funding.

In my view, the best approach is a shared-cost model rather than either extreme. Students who invest in their own education tend to be more motivated and more selective about their courses, and institutions with reliable income can maintain high standards. However, this system works only if means-tested scholarships guarantee that no capable applicant is deterred by financial hardship.

In conclusion, although free education has undeniable appeal on grounds of equality, I believe that a balanced system combining personal contribution with strong financial support offers a fairer and more durable solution for both individuals and society.

As digital payment systems become ubiquitous, an increasing number of businesses are choosing to operate without cash. In my view, although this trend creates genuine difficulties for some customers, the benefits are greater overall because electronic transactions are faster, safer, and easier to manage for both firms and consumers.

One major advantage of cashless trading is efficiency. Card readers and mobile wallets usually process payments in seconds, which reduces queues and allows staff to serve more people during busy periods. This is particularly valuable in urban coffee shops, supermarkets, and fast-food outlets, where delays at the register can significantly affect customer satisfaction. In addition, digital payments simplify accounting because each sale is recorded automatically, reducing human error and making it easier for owners to monitor revenue, calculate taxes, and identify suspicious transactions. A small restaurant, for example, can reconcile its daily takings almost instantly instead of counting notes and coins by hand after closing.

A second benefit is improved security. Cash can be stolen by thieves, misplaced by employees, or lost without any possibility of recovery. By contrast, electronic payments leave a trace, and banks can often block fraudulent activity or return funds in disputed cases. Cashless premises may therefore become less attractive targets for robbery, especially late at night. This is a significant advantage for convenience stores or takeout restaurants operating in high-crime areas, where reducing the amount of money kept on site can protect both workers and owners.

Nevertheless, refusing cash altogether does have drawbacks. It may exclude elderly people, those on very low incomes, or anyone without a bank account or smartphone. Technical failures are another concern: if payment networks crash, customers may be unable to buy essential goods. Even so, these problems can be mitigated through basic policy measures, such as maintaining low-cost bank access and keeping emergency backup systems.

Overall, the move toward card and phone payments is beneficial despite its disadvantages. While some groups need better support during the transition, the gains in speed, security, and administrative convenience mean that the advantages do, on balance, outweigh the disadvantages.

Rising levels of excess weight are now evident on every continent, and the trend has alarmed health authorities everywhere. In my view, the problem stems chiefly from changes in diet and in daily routines, and it can best be tackled through a combination of stricter food regulation and the deliberate promotion of active living.

The first major cause is the widespread availability of cheap, calorie-dense processed food. Products such as sugary drinks, packaged snacks, and fast-food meals are aggressively marketed, conveniently located, and often less expensive than fresh vegetables or lean protein. Consequently, families on tight budgets frequently consume more energy than their bodies require. In Mexico, for instance, the rapid spread of soft drinks into even remote villages has coincided with a steep increase in obesity and diabetes.

A second cause is the decline in physical activity. Modern employment is increasingly sedentary, with millions of people spending their working days at computers, and leisure time is often absorbed by screens rather than sports or outdoor play. Urban design compounds the problem, because cities built around cars discourage walking and cycling. Children who are driven to school and then spend the evening gaming, for example, may burn far fewer calories than previous generations did.

Several measures could reverse this trend. Governments should impose taxes on sugary products and restrict advertising aimed at children, while using the revenue to subsidize healthy staples. Britain's levy on sugar-sweetened drinks prompted manufacturers to reformulate their recipes, which shows that such policies can work. In addition, schools and municipalities should encourage exercise by providing compulsory physical education, safe cycle lanes, and accessible public parks. Equally important, nutrition education should teach people to read food labels and cook inexpensive, balanced meals at home.

In conclusion, the growing number of overweight people reflects an environment that makes unhealthy eating easy and physical activity optional. Only coordinated action, combining fiscal measures, public education, and better urban planning, is likely to reverse the trend.

The growing preference for online shopping is mainly driven by convenience, wider choice, and lower prices, and this shift is reshaping town centers in significant ways. In my view, while consumers benefit enormously from digital retail, the long-term effect on urban commercial districts is largely negative unless those areas adapt to new patterns of demand.

The primary reason people increasingly buy goods online is that internet platforms make shopping faster and easier than visiting physical stores. Consumers can compare prices within minutes, read reviews from other buyers, and place orders at any hour without traveling or waiting in line. Online retailers also tend to offer a broader range of products than small local outlets, especially in specialist categories such as electronics, books, or niche clothing sizes. This is often combined with aggressive discounting because digital businesses have lower overhead costs. For example, a parent looking for school supplies can order everything from uniforms to calculators in one transaction and have the items delivered the next day.

This change has had a profound effect on town centers because traditional shops lose foot traffic when purchases move online. As fewer people visit main shopping streets, independent retailers often struggle to cover rent and staffing costs, leading to vacant storefronts and a visible decline in commercial vitality. Once this process begins, it can become self-reinforcing: fewer stores attract fewer visitors, which then harms nearby cafes and service businesses. In many medium-sized towns, former retail hubs now contain shuttered premises that make the area feel neglected and economically fragile.

However, the impact is not entirely destructive if town centers evolve. Physical retail spaces can survive by offering what websites cannot: personal service, immediate access to goods, social interaction, and attractive leisure experiences. Bookstores that host events, food markets featuring local producers, and mixed-use districts with restaurants and cultural venues can still draw substantial crowds. Therefore, although online shopping has weakened the traditional role of town centers, it is most damaging where local authorities and businesses fail to reinvent these spaces as social and experiential destinations rather than purely places to buy goods.
